title: Four Beasts, the Ancient of Days, and the Son of Man
summary: Daniel sees four terrible beasts rise from a storm-tossed sea, the last with ten horns and a boastful little horn. Then thrones are set, the Ancient of Days takes his seat, the court sits in judgment, and the beast is destroyed. One like a son of man comes with the clouds of heaven and receives an everlasting kingdom, which an interpreter explains is given to the saints of the Most High after a time of persecution.
story: This is the hinge of the book. It is the last chapter in Aramaic and so completes the unit that began in chapter 2, whose four-part statue it retells as four beasts. But it is also the first of Daniel's own visions, turning from stories about him to revelations given to him. It steps back in time to the first year of Belshazzar, before the events of chapter 5. Where chapter 2 showed the kingdoms as a statue admired by a king, chapter 7 shows them as God sees them: predatory beasts. And where chapter 2 ended with a stone, this chapter ends with a person. The kingdom that will replace the empires is given to one like a son of man and shared with God's holy people. The visions of chapters 8 to 12 all build on this one.
historical:
Belshazzar's first year was probably in the early 550s BC, when Nabonidus left him in charge of Babylon. The empire still looked secure, though Cyrus of Persia was rising.

The four beasts are explained only as four kings or kingdoms (verses 17 and 23). The first, a lion with eagle's wings that is made to stand like a man and given a human mind, is widely taken as Babylon, recalling Nebuchadnezzar's humbling in chapter 4; Jeremiah had compared Nebuchadnezzar to both a lion and an eagle. The traditional Christian reading then takes the bear as Media-Persia (raised on one side because Persia dominated the Medes), the four-headed leopard as Greece (Alexander's swift conquest and its later division), and the fourth beast as Rome. Most critical scholars read the bear as Media, the leopard as Persia (four heads for four Persian kings, compare 11:2), and the fourth beast as the Greek empire of Alexander and his successors, with the ten horns as Seleucid rulers and the little horn as Antiochus IV, who persecuted the Jews and tried to change their calendar and law (verse 25). Futurist interpreters add that the little horn is a final antichrist figure yet to come. The strengths of each reading are set out in the book introduction.
cultural:
The sea churned by the four winds draws on an image widespread in the ancient Near East and in the Old Testament: the sea as a symbol of chaos and hostile power (Psalm 74:13; Isaiah 27:1). Beasts that combine features of different animals were familiar from Babylonian and Assyrian art, where winged lions and bulls guarded palace gates. To a reader in Babylon, the vision took the empire's own symbols of power and turned them into monsters.

The heavenly courtroom scene uses royal and legal imagery. Thrones are set, the judge takes his seat, the attendants number thousands upon thousands, and books are opened, the records by which the court decides. The Ancient of Days, an aged figure with white clothing and hair like wool, conveys dignity, wisdom, and eternity, and his fiery throne with wheels recalls Ezekiel's vision of God's chariot-throne (Ezekiel 1). The phrase son of man in Aramaic ordinarily means simply a human being. What is remarkable is that this human figure comes with the clouds of heaven, which elsewhere in the Old Testament are the vehicle of God himself (Psalm 104:3; Isaiah 19:1), and receives the worship-like service of all peoples.
literary: The chapter is an apocalyptic vision followed by an interpretation, the pattern for the rest of the book. Daniel sees, is troubled, asks one of the heavenly attendants, and receives an explanation. The vision itself alternates between earth and heaven: beasts rising from the sea (verses 2 to 8), the court in heaven (verses 9 and 10), the beast destroyed (verses 11 and 12), and the son of man enthroned (verses 13 and 14). Parts of the heavenly scenes are written as poetry. The interpretation comes in two rounds, a brief one (verses 17 and 18) and a longer one focused on the fourth beast and the little horn (verses 19 to 27). The repeated contrast is between beastly rule, which devours and tramples, and human rule, which receives its kingdom from God. The phrase "a time, and times, and half a time" (verse 25), usually taken as three and a half years, marks a limited period of suffering.

outline.t: Four beasts from the sea and the little horn
The Ancient of Days and the court in heaven
One like the Son of Man receives the kingdom
The fourth beast, the little horn, and the saints

doctrines.note: History is not left to the beasts. A heavenly court sits, the books are opened, and the arrogant power is condemned. God's judgment is presented as the necessary condition for justice to the oppressed.

The kingdom is given to one like a son of man, a human figure who comes with the clouds and receives everlasting dominion. Later Jewish and Christian readers took him as the Messiah, and Jesus claimed the title for himself.

The kingdom that replaces the empires belongs to God, is given to the son of man, and is shared with "the saints of the Most High" (verses 18, 22, 27). It is everlasting and universal, the opposite of the beasts' temporary dominion.
The saints are handed over to the little horn for a limited time before the court acts (verse 25). The vision does not promise escape from persecution but an end to it and a kingdom beyond it.

words.note: Enash, man or mankind. Joined with bar (son) in verse 13, bar enash is an ordinary Aramaic way of saying a human being. Its force here comes from the contrast with the beasts: God's kingdom is given to a figure who is truly human, not beastly, yet who comes from heaven's side.

Attiq, ancient or advanced in age, used only in this chapter in the title Ancient of Days. It portrays God as eternal and venerable, the judge who was there before every empire and will be there after them.

Qaddish, holy. The holy ones or saints of the Most High receive the kingdom. The same word describes angels in 4:13, and some scholars think the saints here are angelic beings, but most read them as God's faithful people on earth, since they are persecuted by the little horn.

Sholtan, dominion or rule. The beasts' dominion is taken away (verses 12 and 26), while the son of man receives "an everlasting dominion that will not pass away" (verse 14). The chapter is a contest over who holds dominion.

christ: Jesus' favorite way of referring to himself was the Son of Man, and this chapter is its main source. At his trial, when the high priest asked whether he was the Christ, Jesus answered, "I am," and added, "you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power and coming with the clouds of heaven" (Mark 14:62), joining Psalm 110 to Daniel 7:13. The high priest heard it as blasphemy, because Jesus was claiming the place beside God that Daniel gives to the one who comes with the clouds. Jesus also spoke of the Son of Man coming in the clouds with great power and glory (Mark 13:26), and after his resurrection he declared that all authority in heaven and on earth had been given to him (Matthew 28:18), language close to verse 14. The title held together his humility and his glory: an ordinary phrase for a human being that, through Daniel, also named the one who receives God's everlasting kingdom. Stephen at his death saw "the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God" (Acts 7:56), and Revelation describes the risen Christ in terms drawn from both the son of man and the Ancient of Days (Revelation 1:13-14).

hard.q: Who is the one like a son of man?
hard.a: Three main readings are held. Many critical scholars take the figure as a symbol of God's people, since the interpretation says the kingdom is given to the saints of the Most High (verses 18 and 27), just as the beasts symbolize kingdoms. Some scholars take him as an angelic leader of God's people, often identified with Michael, who appears in 10:21 and 12:1. The traditional Jewish and Christian reading, with ancient roots in texts such as the Similitudes of 1 Enoch and 4 Ezra, takes him as an individual heavenly figure, the Messiah, who represents and rules the saints. These readings are not entirely exclusive: a king can represent his people, so the son of man can be an individual whose kingdom his people share. What sets the figure apart is that he comes with the clouds, as God does, and receives service from all peoples. The New Testament confesses that Jesus is this figure, fully human and sharing God's throne.

questions: Daniel sees the great empires as beasts rather than as the statue of chapter 2. What changes when you see power from God's point of view rather than the world's?
The saints suffer for a time before the court sits. How does knowing that suffering has a limit, and a judge, help believers endure it?
Jesus chose the title Son of Man more than any other. What does it say about him that his favorite title could mean both a human being and the one who receives God's kingdom?
